name: Heracles's birth: three nights long and the cradle-snakes
scope: The origin story that opens every Heracles tale. T1: HERACLES ('Glory of Hera' -- the ironic name, because Hera hates him) is the son of ZEUS and the mortal princess ALCMENE of Thebes, wife of the Theban general AMPHITRYON. Zeus wants Alcmene and knows Amphitryon is away at war, so on the night of Amphitryon's return he takes the shape of Amphitryon himself -- and orders HELIOS the sun-god not to rise, making the night THREE NIGHTS LONG so he can lie with her at leisure (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.8). T2: Alcmene therefore bears TWINS with two different fathers -- HERACLES by Zeus and IPHICLES by the real Amphitryon, the same night -- an unusual condition called heteropaternal superfecundation. T3: HERA, Zeus's wife, is furious and tries to prevent the birth: she sends the birth-goddess EILEITHYIA to sit outside the door with her legs crossed and her fingers laced, magically holding the baby in. Alcmene's clever servant GALANTHIS (or Galinthias) runs out and shouts that the baby has already been born; Eileithyia jumps up in shock and breaks the spell, and Heracles is born (Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.281-323). T4: still furious, Hera sends TWO GIANT SNAKES into the cradle to kill the eight-month-old baby. Iphicles screams; Heracles GRABS ONE SNAKE IN EACH HAND and strangles them, and his terrified nurse finds him lying in the cradle playing with two dead serpents (Pindar, Nemean 1.35-50; Apollodorus 2.4.8). T5: it is this failed cradle-attack that first proves he is Zeus's son -- and it foreshadows every labor to come: he will strangle the NEMEAN LION bare-handed just as he strangled the snakes, and everything Hera sends against him will fail. His very name 'Glory of Hera' (Hera-kles) is the story's dark joke: he becomes glorious only because Hera keeps trying to kill him and keeps making him do impossible things. Further rungs: his real Theban tutor was LINUS, whom he later killed by hitting him over the head with the lyre during a music lesson; his archery tutor was EURYTUS (whose own daughter Iole he would later love); the twelve labors are set by his cousin EURYSTHEUS of Mycenae, thanks to Hera again -- she tricks Zeus into swearing that whichever descendant of Perseus is born next will rule, and then speeds Eurystheus's birth while delaying Heracles's.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.5-2.4.8 (Zeus disguised as Amphitryon, the three-night trick, twin birth with Iphicles, Hera sending the two snakes, the eight-month-old Heracles strangling them); Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.281-323 (Alcmene's own retelling of Galanthis and the crossed legs of Eileithyia); Pindar, Nemean 1.35-72 (the cradle-snakes scene at length); Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 4.9-4.10. DISTRACTOR MINE: other snake-killers (Apollo at Delphi killing Python, baby Perseus in the chest is a different story), other Zeus-mortal sons (Perseus by Danae, Dionysus by Semele -- adjacent-real, must be distinguished), other 'strangled bare-handed' scenes (the Nemean Lion later in the same cycle). name: Labor 1: the Nemean Lion strangled bare-handed
scope: The first of the twelve labors. T1: after Hera drives him mad and he kills his own wife MEGARA and their children, Heracles goes to the ORACLE AT DELPHI to atone; the Pythia tells him to serve his cousin EURYSTHEUS of Mycenae for ten years and do whatever tasks the king sets. Eurystheus, a coward, sets him TWELVE LABORS meant to be fatal (Apollodorus 2.5.1). T2: the FIRST LABOR is to kill the NEMEAN LION, a monstrous beast whose HIDE cannot be pierced by any weapon -- its skin turns aside bronze, iron and stone. It has been eating the people of Nemea in the north Peloponnese. T3: Heracles finds the lion in a cave with TWO ENTRANCES; he blocks up one entrance with boulders, goes in through the other, and finds his arrows bounce off the golden hide. T4: he DROPS HIS WEAPONS entirely -- club, bow, sword -- and STRANGLES the lion with his BARE ARMS around its neck. T5: because no blade will cut the hide, he skins the lion using ONE OF ITS OWN CLAWS, and from then on wears the LION SKIN as his cloak, with the head as a hood (this is how he appears in every subsequent labor, in vase-painting and sculpture -- lion-skin, club, bow). The invulnerable pelt makes him arrow-proof and sword-proof for the rest of the cycle. Further rungs: the lion is said to be the offspring of ORTHRUS (Geryon's two-headed dog) and Echidna in some sources, or of Typhon in others; when the beast is dead its image is placed in the sky as the constellation LEO; Eurystheus is so terrified when Heracles carries the corpse home that he hides in a bronze jar sunk into the ground and orders Heracles never again to enter the city -- from now on labors are delivered through a herald.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.1 (the labor, the impenetrable hide, the two-mouthed cave, blocking one entrance, strangling bare-handed, skinning with the claw, Eurystheus hiding in the jar); Hesiod, Theogony 326-332 (the lion as offspring of Orthrus and Echidna); Theocritus, Idyll 25 (the whole hunt in verse); Diodorus 4.11. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (he dropped all his WEAPONS and choked it to death with his ARMS) and T5 (nothing could cut its hide -- so he skinned it with its OWN CLAW). Wrong tools: not a sword (bounced), not an arrow (bounced), not the club (some sources include the club, but the KILL is strangulation).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Nemea as a Peloponnesian place with its own ancient games; theology owns the lion story. ANIMAL bank owns real lions in the ancient Mediterranean; theology owns the monstrous invulnerable lion of the story.

name: Labor 2: the Lernaean Hydra and Iolaus with the torch
scope: The labor that requires a helper and starts the Hydra-poison arc. T1: the SECOND LABOR is the LERNAEAN HYDRA, a many-headed water-serpent that lives in the swamp of LERNA in the Argolid and comes out to burn the crops and eat the cattle. Some sources say nine heads, some say more; one of them is IMMORTAL (Apollodorus 2.5.2). T2: Heracles arrives with his nephew and charioteer IOLAUS. When he cuts off one head with his sword, TWO NEW HEADS grow back from the stump -- the fight is unwinnable one-cut-at-a-time. T3: to make it worse, Hera sends a giant CRAB up out of the swamp to bite Heracles's foot; he crushes the crab (its image goes into the sky as the constellation CANCER) and calls to Iolaus for help. T4: Iolaus takes a burning FIREBRAND (or, in some versions, sets fire to a grove nearby) and, as Heracles slices off each head, CAUTERIZES THE STUMP with the flame so no new heads can grow. Head after head, the two of them clear it. T5: the last, IMMORTAL head is buried under a huge ROCK by the road; and Heracles dips his ARROWS in the Hydra's blood -- from now on his arrows carry an incurable POISON that will decide many of the later stories (Nessus the centaur will die of it, Chiron the tutor of Jason will accidentally die of it, and Heracles himself will finally die of it through the shirt of Nessus). Because Iolaus HELPED, Eurystheus refuses to count this labor and gives him an extra to make twelve, not ten. Further rungs: the Hydra's father is said to be TYPHON and mother Echidna, making her a sibling of the Nemean Lion and Cerberus; Hera puts the Hydra herself into the sky as the constellation HYDRA; a vase in the British Museum shows exactly the crab biting the ankle while a small Iolaus applies a torch to a spurting stump.

name: Labor 3: the Ceryneian Hind of Artemis
scope: The gentler labor with the delicate diplomatic ending. T1: the THIRD LABOR is to bring back ALIVE the CERYNEIAN HIND, a deer with GOLDEN HORNS and BRONZE HOOVES (or in some sources HOOVES OF BRASS) that is sacred to ARTEMIS. It can outrun an arrow. T2: because the hind must be captured LIVING and unharmed, Heracles cannot use his poisoned arrows or his club; his task is to catch a creature faster than his weapons. T3: he chases the hind for a WHOLE YEAR through Greece and Thrace, all the way to the land of the HYPERBOREANS in the far north (Apollodorus 2.5.3), and finally corners her; some sources say he wounds her with a light arrow through both forelegs so no blood is shed, others that he catches her sleeping in a thicket, others that he nets her by a river. T4: on the way back through Arcadia, ARTEMIS and her brother APOLLO meet him and demand to know why he is carrying off her sacred deer; Heracles apologizes, explains Eurystheus set the labor, promises to return the hind alive, and Artemis lets him pass. T5: at Mycenae he shows the hind to Eurystheus; the king demands the deer be kept in the royal menagerie, and Heracles, keeping his promise to Artemis, RELEASES her as soon as Eurystheus has looked -- so the labor is 'delivered' but Artemis's animal is not lost. This is the ONLY labor where the target lives at the end. Further rungs: the hind is sometimes identified as one of five golden-horned deer Artemis originally caught to draw her chariot -- four became her chariot-team, and this fifth escaped and became the Ceryneian; the mountain of Ceryneia lies between Achaea and Arcadia; the Homeric Hymn to Artemis (Hymn 27) sings of her chariot pulled by golden-horned deer, connecting the wider herd.

Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the ONLY labor where the target lived; Heracles let it go after showing Eurystheus) and T3 (he chased it for a WHOLE YEAR, all the way to the far-north Hyperboreans). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Fionn hunting the enchanted deer that was really Sadhbh, or of the White Hart in Arthurian romance -- the sacred beast that must be caught but not harmed. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Artemis-sacred creatures (her wild boars, her bears, the Actaeon-stag), other 'must be brought alive' labors (the Erymanthian Boar, the Cretan Bull -- adjacent labors, all three ALIVE), other labors with a divine encounter mid-return (the Hesperides with Atlas, Cerberus with Hades). name: Labor 4: the Erymanthian Boar and the snow-drift
scope: The labor with the throwaway funny ending. T1: the FOURTH LABOR is to bring back ALIVE the ERYMANTHIAN BOAR, a massive tusked beast the size of a bull that has been ravaging the fields on the flanks of Mount ERYMANTHOS in Arcadia. T2: on the way, Heracles stops with the wise centaur PHOLUS, who serves him roasted meat but hesitates to open a jar of centaur wine, saying it belongs to all the centaurs in common; Heracles opens it anyway, the smell brings the other centaurs down the mountain armed with rocks and pine trees, and a huge brawl breaks out (Apollodorus 2.5.4). Heracles fires his Hydra-poisoned arrows; the centaurs scatter and flee to their wise elder CHIRON. T3: one of Heracles's arrows misses its target and hits CHIRON in the knee -- Chiron, who is immortal, cannot die but cannot heal the Hydra-poison either; he suffers agony until Prometheus later agrees to trade his immortality for Chiron's, so Chiron can finally die (this is how Prometheus, the fire-thief, becomes 'immortal', by inheriting an immortality from Chiron). Pholus meanwhile drops one of the poisoned arrows on his own foot by accident and dies of the scratch. T4: Heracles goes on and finds the boar high in the mountains; the trick is that the beast is huge but ALIVE-capture is impossible in a fair fight. He drives the boar UPHILL, into DEEP SNOW, and the animal sinks belly-deep and cannot move. He then binds it in chains. T5: he carries the enormous bound boar back to Mycenae on his shoulders and dumps it in front of the palace -- and this is the moment EURYSTHEUS panics and HIDES IN THE BRONZE JAR sunk in the ground (the same jar he first used after the Nemean Lion), calling out his orders through a herald from inside. In Greek vase-painting this scene -- king in the jar, Heracles hoisting a bound boar over his head -- is one of the most-painted Heracles moments. Further rungs: Chiron the wise centaur who accidentally dies of the poison is the same Chiron who tutored Jason, Achilles, Asclepius, and other heroes; Prometheus's freeing (Heracles later shoots the eagle at Prometheus's liver) is directly linked to this arrow-wound, since Prometheus inherits Chiron's immortality; the boar's tusks were said to be preserved and shown at the temple of Apollo at Cumae in Italy centuries later.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.4 (Pholus and the centaur wine, the brawl with the poisoned arrows, Chiron's accidental wound, Pholus dropping the arrow, the boar driven into deep snow and bound alive, Eurystheus hiding in the jar); Diodorus 4.12; Pausanias 8.24.5 (the boar's tusks at Cumae in later report). name: Labor 5: the Augean Stables and the two rivers
scope: The dirtiest labor and the wildest solution. T1: the FIFTH LABOR is to CLEAN THE STABLES of King AUGEAS of ELIS in ONE DAY. Augeas owns the largest herd of cattle in Greece -- thousands of divinely-immortal cattle -- and their stables have not been cleaned in THIRTY YEARS. The dung is so deep that the surrounding fields have become uncultivable. Eurystheus meant it as a HUMILIATION as much as a physical impossibility (Apollodorus 2.5.5). T2: Heracles goes to Augeas and offers to clean the stables in one day in exchange for a TENTH OF THE CATTLE; Augeas laughs and agrees, thinking the offer impossible. T3: Heracles then goes to the walls of the cattle-yard and TEARS AN OPENING in the wall on the upstream side and another on the downstream side. T4: he DIVERTS THE COURSES OF TWO RIVERS -- the ALPHEUS and the PENEUS (some sources say the Menius alongside the Alpheus) -- so that they flow straight through the stables, washing thirty years of dung out downstream in a single day; then he closes the gaps and lets the rivers return to their beds. T5: Augeas, when he hears the labor was done for hire, refuses the payment; his own son PHYLEUS testifies against him and is banished for it; Heracles later returns with an army, kills Augeas and puts Phyleus on the throne. And Eurystheus refuses to count this labor also, because Heracles was going to be PAID for it -- so between Iolaus at the Hydra and this hired labor, he now owes TWO EXTRA labors to make the count reach twelve. Further rungs: after killing Augeas, Heracles is said to have founded the OLYMPIC GAMES at Olympia on the banks of the Alpheus, in gratitude for the labor and the victory; the herd is described in Theocritus's Idyll 25 as three thousand cattle, three hundred of them white as milk, twelve of them the sacred bulls of Helios the sun-god (Augeas himself was a son of Helios); the Peneus and Alpheus are still-existing rivers of the western Peloponnese today.

name: Labor 6: the Stymphalian birds and the bronze rattle
scope: The labor with the noise-maker. T1: the SIXTH LABOR is to drive off the STYMPHALIAN BIRDS, a flock of man-eating birds that has taken over the marshes of LAKE STYMPHALIA in Arcadia. Their FEATHERS are of BRONZE (they can shoot them like arrows), their BEAKS are of BRONZE, and their DROPPINGS are poisonous; they hide in the reeds of the swamp where Heracles cannot approach on foot. T2: the birds are so many they blot out the sun when they take to the air, and they refuse to fly -- they stay hidden in the marsh where an arrow cannot find them. T3: Heracles is stumped by the terrain until ATHENA appears and gives him a great BRONZE RATTLE (a 'krotala', in some sources a pair of bronze castanets) made by HEPHAESTUS himself, on Mount Olympus. T4: Heracles climbs a nearby hill and CLASHES THE RATTLE -- the terrible noise startles the birds into the air all at once. T5: as they rise in a great cloud, Heracles shoots them out of the sky one by one with his Hydra-poisoned arrows; many are killed, the survivors flee across the Black Sea to the island of ARES (where they later attack Jason and the Argonauts, who drive them off by clashing their shields the same way -- Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 2.1030-1089 explicitly reuses Heracles's trick). Further rungs: the birds are said to have been sacred to Ares, god of war, which is why the survivors flee to his island; the rattle-and-birds scene is one of the very few labors where a god actively helps Heracles (Athena, again, as she helps every young hero); Pausanias 8.22 reports the temple of Artemis Stymphalia at the lake had reliefs of the birds still visible in the 2nd century CE.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.6 (Athena giving the bronze rattle made by Hephaestus, Heracles shaking it, birds startled up, shot with arrows); Pausanias 8.22.4-5 (temple of Artemis Stymphalia, reliefs of the birds); Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 2.1030-1089 (the Argonauts reusing the same trick with clashing shields against the survivors on the island of Ares). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Athena gave him a BRONZE RATTLE forged by Hephaestus to scare them out of the swamp) and T1 (their FEATHERS and BEAKS were of BRONZE and their droppings were POISON). name: Labor 7: the Cretan Bull that Minos would not sacrifice
scope: The bull that ties into Minos, Pasiphae, and eventually the Minotaur. T1: the SEVENTH LABOR is to capture ALIVE the CRETAN BULL, a magnificent white bull that is running wild on the island of CRETE and destroying the fields. T2: the bull's backstory is famous: POSEIDON sent it from the sea as a sign that King MINOS was the rightful king of Crete, on the promise that Minos would sacrifice it back to him. When Minos saw how beautiful the bull was, he KEPT IT and sacrificed an ordinary bull in its place. Poseidon in anger drove the bull mad and made MINOS'S WIFE PASIPHAE fall in love with it -- and their union (with the help of Daedalus's wooden cow) produced the MINOTAUR (Apollodorus 3.1.4). So this labor's bull is the FATHER of the Minotaur. T3: Heracles arrives at the court of Minos and asks for help capturing the beast; Minos refuses to help, still guilty about his broken promise, but tells Heracles he may take the bull if he can catch it. T4: Heracles WRESTLES the bull to the ground bare-handed (there are vase-paintings of exactly this pose -- hero on the bull's back, one arm hooked over the horn), binds it, and carries it back on his shoulders across the sea to Mycenae. T5: Eurystheus dedicates the bull to HERA, but Hera refuses the gift (she does not want anything from Heracles). She releases the bull, which wanders through the Peloponnese and eventually settles on the plain of MARATHON in Attica, where it becomes known as the MARATHONIAN BULL -- and is finally killed by THESEUS in one of his own early labors (see the Theseus strand). So the Cretan Bull passes from Heracles's story into Theseus's. Further rungs: the Minotaur (child of Pasiphae and this bull) is the same monster Theseus later kills in the Labyrinth; some sources conflate this bull with the white bull that carried Europa to Crete originally (Zeus's own disguise); the whole cycle -- Zeus as bull, Cretan bull, Marathonian bull, Minotaur -- is Crete's bull-obsession in mythical form.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.7 (the labor) and 3.1.4 (Minos's broken promise, Poseidon's anger, Pasiphae's love, the origin of the Minotaur); Diodorus 4.13.4; Pausanias 1.27.10 (the Marathonian bull as later killed by Theseus). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Cretan Bull' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Cretan Bull', 'Minotaur', 'Pasiphae' -- Poseidon sending the bull as sign, Minos keeping it, Pasiphae's love and the Minotaur origin, Heracles wrestling and shipping the bull, Hera refusing the dedication, the bull wandering to Marathon, Theseus later killing it.
framing_note: The 'bull with a backstory' ladder -- the Minotaur-parentage is the payoff most kids don't know. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (this bull is the FATHER OF THE MINOTAUR -- Poseidon's punishment of Minos was making his wife fall in love with the bull he had refused to sacrifice) and T5 (Heracles's bull was released, wandered to Marathon, and was later killed by THESEUS -- one hero's labor becomes the next hero's labor). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name the Minotaur AND ask whose father it was -- describe the SCENE (a white bull sent from the sea, a king who kept it, a queen who fell in love with it) and let the recall be the OFFSPRING (Minotaur), the KING (Minos), or the later killer (Theseus). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of the Norse cycle where one artifact passes hero-to-hero (Odin's spear, the ring Andvaranaut), or of the Grail passing from Joseph of Arimathea through Fisher King to Galahad -- an object with a long journey. DISTRACTOR MINE: other bulls (Zeus as bull carrying Europa; the bulls of Geryon; the fire-breathing bulls of Aeetes that Jason yokes -- adjacent-real from same strand, must be distinguished), other Minos stories, other Poseidon-sea-monsters (Cetus who attacks Andromeda -- also Poseidon-sent, adjacent). Wrong killers of the Marathonian bull: not Heracles (he only captured it), not Perseus; THESEUS killed it.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Crete and Marathon as real places; theology owns the bull-cycle story. HISTORY owns Bronze-Age Crete with its bull-leaping frescoes; theology owns the Minotaur cycle. THESEUS's Marathonian-Bull labor is covered in a separate rung of the Theseus ladder here.

name: Labor 8: the man-eating mares of Diomedes
scope: The horse-taming labor with the horror twist. T1: the EIGHTH LABOR is to bring back the MARES OF DIOMEDES, four wild horses belonging to King DIOMEDES of THRACE (not the Diomedes at Troy -- a different king). The mares are MAN-EATERS: Diomedes has been feeding them on the flesh of unlucky travellers and shipwrecked strangers, and the taste has driven them wild. T2: their names in some sources are PODARGOS ('swift-foot'), LAMPON ('shining'), XANTHOS ('yellow'), and DEINOS ('terrible'); they are chained with iron chains to bronze mangers because no rope will hold them. T3: Heracles sails to Thrace with a small band of companions, including his young friend ABDERUS (some sources say his lover, some his squire). They surprise the mares in the stable, break the chains, and drive the horses down to the shore. T4: Diomedes and his Bistones (his tribe) come after them in force. Heracles leaves ABDERUS holding the mares while he goes back to fight, KILLS Diomedes, and returns to find that the mares have EATEN HIS FRIEND. In grief he founds the city of ABDERA on the spot in his friend's honor. He then FEEDS DIOMEDES HIMSELF to the mares -- and, having tasted their own master, they become calm and controllable (Apollodorus 2.5.8). T5: he leads the tame mares back to Mycenae. Eurystheus dedicates them to Hera as before; Hera again refuses; the mares are released into the wild on Mount OLYMPUS where WOLVES eventually eat them -- another Hera-cursed dedication turned loose. In some sources their bloodline lives on as the wild horses of Thrace and produced the horses of Bucephalus centuries later (Alexander the Great's mount was said to descend from them). Further rungs: the city of Abdera was a real Greek colony on the Thracian coast (birthplace of the philosophers Democritus and Protagoras) and traced its foundation story to Heracles's friend; the labor is the last land-labor in the mainland-Greek group -- the next three (Hippolyta, Geryon, Hesperides) will take him to the ends of the world.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.8 (Thracian Diomedes, four mares chained with iron to bronze mangers, feeding on flesh, Abderus killed, city of Abdera founded, Diomedes fed to the mares, mares tamed after eating their master, later released and eaten by wolves on Olympus); Diodorus 4.15; Euripides, Alcestis 481-506 (Heracles on his way to Diomedes stops at Admetus's palace); Strabo 7.331 (Abdera named after Heracles's friend). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Mares of Diomedes' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Mares of Diomedes', 'Abderus' -- Diomedes of Thrace (not the Trojan Diomedes), man-eating mares fed on strangers, iron chains and bronze mangers, Heracles's friend Abderus eaten, city of Abdera founded in his memory, Diomedes fed to his own horses, mares tamed after that, later escaped and eaten by wolves. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the four names (Podargos, Lampon, Xanthos, Deinos) are in Apollodorus specifically or a later source.
framing_note: The 'feed the tyrant to his own horses' ladder -- the poetic-justice reveal is the dinner-test hook. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Heracles fed the KING to his own MAN-EATING HORSES and only then did they become calm) and T1 (a king had been feeding travellers to his own horses). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem describe man-eating horses AND ask what Heracles did with Diomedes -- describe the SCENE (a Thracian king, iron chains, a lover left to guard the horses) and let the recall be the ACT (fed the king to them), the fate of the FRIEND (Abderus eaten, city named for him), or the number of mares (four). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Perillos the bronze-smith burned in his own hollow bull, or of Haman hung on his own gallows (Esther) -- the tyrant destroyed by his own instrument. Kids can handle it. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Diomedes (the Greek warrior at Troy -- adjacent-real, must be distinguished), other man-eating creatures (the Nemean Lion, the Stymphalian Birds, the mares -- all adjacent labors), other named-horse groups (the horses of Achilles, Xanthus and Balius; the horses of the sun -- adjacent-real). Wrong friend: not Iolaus (survives the whole cycle), not Hylas (drowns on the Argo voyage); Abderus is the one eaten here.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Thrace and the real Greek colony of Abdera; theology owns the founding-legend and the mares. HISTORY owns Democritus of Abdera as philosopher; theology owns why the city bears his name.

name: Labor 9: the girdle of Hippolyta the Amazon
scope: The labor set for Eurystheus's daughter and undone by Hera. T1: the NINTH LABOR is to bring back the GIRDLE (Greek 'zoster' -- more properly a war-belt than a modern girdle) of HIPPOLYTA, queen of the AMAZONS, a tribe of warrior women living beyond the Black Sea on the river THERMODON with their capital at THEMISCYRA. The girdle was given to Hippolyta by her father ARES, god of war, as a token of her authority. T2: Eurystheus wants the girdle as a present for his daughter ADMETE, a priestess of Hera. Heracles sails with a small band (in some sources including THESEUS in his youth). T3: they arrive at Themiscyra and Hippolyta comes out to meet them -- she is impressed by Heracles, welcomes him, and AGREES TO GIVE HIM THE GIRDLE WILLINGLY. It is a peaceful diplomatic labor -- for one moment (Apollodorus 2.5.9). T4: then HERA, disguised as an Amazon, runs among the Amazons crying that Heracles is stealing their queen; the Amazons take up arms and rush the Greek ships. Heracles, believing Hippolyta betrayed him, KILLS HIPPOLYTA, takes the girdle, and fights his way back to sea. T5: on the voyage home he stops at TROY, where he finds the daughter of King LAOMEDON -- HESIONE -- chained to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea-monster sent by Poseidon (Laomedon had cheated Poseidon over the building of the walls). Heracles kills the sea-monster and saves Hesione, but Laomedon cheats HIM too by withholding the promised horses; Heracles later returns with an army, sacks Troy the first time, kills Laomedon, and gives Hesione as bride to his friend TELAMON -- their son will be AJAX THE GREAT of the Trojan War. So this labor doubles as the FIRST SACK OF TROY, before the famous Trojan War of Homer. Further rungs: the girdle is given by Eurystheus to Admete as intended, and in some versions the Amazon captive TAKEN AS PLUNDER is Hippolyta's sister ANTIOPE, whom Theseus later marries -- provoking the Amazon invasion of Attica; Homer's Iliad refers back to Heracles's earlier sack of Troy in the mouths of Priam and Hera; Hera's disguise-and-rumor trick echoes her other cycle-shaping interventions.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9 (the girdle labor, Hippolyta willing to give it, Hera disguised as an Amazon starting the rumor, Heracles killing Hippolyta, stopping at Troy on the way home, saving Hesione from the sea-monster, Laomedon's cheat, the first sack of Troy); Homer, Iliad 5.640-651 (Tlepolemus reminding Sarpedon of Heracles's earlier sack of Troy with six ships); Diodorus 4.16; Euripides, Heracles 408-418 (the Amazon expedition). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Hippolyta' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Hippolyta', 'Labours of Heracles', 'Hesione' -- Amazon queen at Themiscyra on the Thermodon, girdle from her father Ares, Eurystheus's daughter Admete wanting it, Hippolyta willing to give it, Hera disguised as an Amazon starting a fight, Hippolyta killed, first sack of Troy on the way home, Hesione saved from the sea-monster, later begetting of Ajax through Telamon.
framing_note: The 'Hera in disguise ruins a peaceful labor' ladder + the surprise sack-of-Troy epilogue. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (HERA in disguise as an Amazon started the battle that killed Hippolyta after she had already AGREED to give the girdle) and T5 (on the way home, Heracles SACKED TROY the first time -- generations before Achilles). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name Hera AND ask who started the battle -- describe the SCENE (a queen willing to give a gift, a whispered rumor, an armed rush to the shore) and let the recall be the SABOTEUR (Hera), the location (Themiscyra on the Thermodon), or the surprise stopover (Troy, saving Hesione). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Loki disguised as an old woman to trick Frigg for the mistletoe secret, or of the Morrigan disguised as an old washerwoman warning Cuchulainn -- goddess-in-disguise as a story-mover. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Amazon queens (Penthesilea killed by Achilles at Troy; Antiope; Melanippe -- adjacent-real, must be distinguished), other Trojan-War sackings (the famous one Homer sings, with Achilles and the horse -- adjacent-real, must be distinguished, this is the EARLIER sack), other 'peaceful labor turns violent' moments. Wrong Amazon river: the Thermodon (right), not the Styx.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Black Sea and the Thermodon as ancient waterways; theology owns Amazon Themiscyra. HISTORY owns Troy as an archaeological site with multiple destruction layers; theology owns Heracles's PRE-Homeric sack (the layer sometimes called Troy VI destruction is separately debated).

name: Labor 10: the cattle of Geryon and the golden cup of Helios
scope: The far-west labor and the pillars of Heracles. T1: the TENTH LABOR is to bring back the CATTLE of GERYON, a monstrous herd of red oxen owned by a three-bodied giant (Apollodorus says three heads joined at the waist and three bodies joined below) named GERYON, who lives on the island of ERYTHEIA ('the red land') at the far western edge of the world, past the ocean-stream that circles the earth. His herdsman is EURYTION and his guard-dog is ORTHRUS, a two-headed hound (the brother of Cerberus, both sons of Typhon and Echidna). T2: to reach the far west Heracles crosses North Africa and Europe; at the strait between Africa and Spain he sets up TWO GREAT MOUNTAIN PILLARS on either side of the strait as the boundary of the known world -- the PILLARS OF HERACLES (the Rock of Gibraltar and Jebel Musa in Morocco, still marking the strait today). Some sources say he ripped one mountain in half to make the strait itself, opening the Mediterranean to the Atlantic (Apollodorus 2.5.10). T3: the SUN is beating down so hard he cannot walk further, so Heracles DRAWS HIS BOW AND AIMS IT AT HELIOS -- the sun-god, impressed by the audacity, gives him the GOLDEN CUP that Helios himself sails home in every night from the west to the east across the ocean-stream (Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 11.469; Apollodorus 2.5.10). Heracles sails to Erytheia in the golden cup. T4: on the island he kills the two-headed dog ORTHRUS with one blow of his club, kills the herdsman EURYTION next, and finally kills GERYON himself with a single Hydra-poisoned arrow that pierces all three bodies at once (Stesichorus's lost poem 'Geryoneis' told this at length; the fragments are our earliest source). T5: he loads the red cattle into the golden cup and sails back east across the ocean; then drives the herd overland the length of Italy (foundation-legends of many Italian sites -- including the future site of ROME -- attach to this trip; the giant CACUS steals cattle from him at the site of Rome and Heracles kills Cacus in a cave, an episode Virgil retells in Aeneid 8.185-275). Hera sends a gadfly to scatter the herd in Thrace; Heracles rounds them up again and brings them to Mycenae, where Eurystheus sacrifices them to Hera. Further rungs: Erytheia is variously located near Cadiz in Spain, in the Iberian Atlantic, or symbolically 'past the sunset'; the golden cup is the same cup in which Helios sleeps every night before rising the next morning from the east; the Cacus episode is why Rome's oldest sacred site, the Ara Maxima in the Forum Boarium, was said by Livy to be an altar to Heracles (Livy 1.7).
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.10 (three-bodied Geryon, Orthrus the two-headed dog, Eurytion the herdsman, Pillars of Heracles, Helios's golden cup after the bow-drawing, the killing with one arrow, the overland return through Italy, Hera's gadfly); Stesichorus, Geryoneis fragments (the fullest early telling); Hesiod, Theogony 287-294 and 979-983 (Geryon as three-headed son of Chrysaor); Virgil, Aeneid 8.185-275 (Cacus, the cave at the future site of Rome); Livy 1.7 (the Ara Maxima). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Geryon' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Geryon', 'Cattle of Geryon', 'Pillars of Heracles' -- three bodies, Erytheia in the far west, Orthrus the two-headed guard-dog, herdsman Eurytion, Pillars set up at the strait (Gibraltar / Jebel Musa), Helios giving the golden cup after Heracles drew a bow at him, killing all three with one poisoned arrow, the return trip through Italy with Cacus at Rome's future site.
framing_note: The 'ends of the earth' labor -- the Helios-cup and Pillars are both dinner-test material. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Heracles pointed his bow AT THE SUN, and the sun-god gave him a golden CUP-SHAPED BOAT to sail west in) and T2 (the two great pillars at the strait between Africa and Spain -- Gibraltar and Jebel Musa -- are STILL CALLED the Pillars of Heracles). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name Helios AND ask which god gave the cup -- describe the SCENE (a hero threatened by unbearable heat drawing his bow) and let the recall be the GOD (Helios), the GIFT (a golden cup that is also a boat), or the location (Erytheia, far west). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Thor waded across the world-sea to Utgard, or of Bran's cauldron voyage west to Ireland, or of the Argonauts sailing past the edge of the known world -- a hero at the world's rim. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Heracles cattle stories (the Augean stables cattle -- adjacent-real from the same cycle; the Cretan Bull), other far-west or far-east labors (the Hesperides with Atlas -- next labor, must be distinguished), other three-bodied or many-headed monsters (Cerberus, the Hydra, Orthrus -- Orthrus IS in this labor). Wrong pillars: the Pillars of Hercules are on either side of the STRAIT OF GIBRALTAR, not at Delphi.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Strait of Gibraltar and the Pillars of Hercules as real geography, and the Forum Boarium in Rome as a real site; theology owns the founding-legends (the strait cut open, the pillars set up, the Ara Maxima). HISTORY owns real early-Rome sacred sites; theology owns Cacus's cave story.

name: Labor 11: the apples of the Hesperides and Atlas's trick
scope: The labor with the cleverest trick. T1: the ELEVENTH LABOR is to bring back the GOLDEN APPLES of the HESPERIDES -- three (or in some sources four) NYMPHS ('daughters of Evening') who tend a magical garden at the far western edge of the world, on the slopes of Mount Atlas. In the garden grows a tree with GOLDEN APPLES, a wedding-present from GAIA to Hera when Hera married Zeus; the tree is guarded by a hundred-headed dragon named LADON who never sleeps (Hesiod, Theogony 215-216, 333-336). T2: Heracles doesn't know where the garden is. On the way he wrestles the sea-god NEREUS in every shape Nereus can change into (fire, water, snake) until Nereus tells him the way -- but adds that the apples can only be picked by ATLAS, the Titan who is holding up the sky at the edge of the world nearby. T3: Heracles finds ATLAS bent under the sky and offers a deal: 'go pick the apples for me and I will hold up the sky while you are gone.' Atlas is delighted -- he has held that sky for thousands of years since the Titanomachy. He gives the whole burden to Heracles and walks off to pick the apples. T4: Atlas comes back with THREE GOLDEN APPLES in his hand and looks at Heracles standing under the sky -- and says, 'Well, since I am up and about, why don't I just carry them to Mycenae for you myself?' -- meaning to leave Heracles holding the sky forever. Heracles, quickly, says: 'Certainly! But first, could you take the sky back JUST FOR A MOMENT, so I can put a pad on my shoulders? It hurts.' Atlas puts the apples on the ground, takes the sky back on his shoulders -- and Heracles picks up the apples and WALKS AWAY, leaving Atlas holding it up again (Apollodorus 2.5.11). T5: he brings the apples to Eurystheus, who cannot keep them (they belong to Hera); Athena eventually takes them back to the garden. Also on the same trip Heracles frees PROMETHEUS from his crag in the Caucasus by shooting the EAGLE that eats the liver every day -- the same trip that pays off the older Prometheus story. Further rungs: the dragon LADON, killed in some versions by Heracles's arrow through the garden wall, is placed in the sky as the constellation DRACO, coiled around the pole; the Hesperides in some sources are Aegle, Erytheia, Hesperia and Arethusa; the location of the garden is variously placed in North Africa near the Atlas Mountains, in Iberia, or beyond the ocean-stream.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.11 (Nereus wrestled for directions, Atlas holding the sky, Heracles offering to hold it, Atlas going to fetch the apples, Atlas trying to leave Heracles with it forever, Heracles's shoulder-pad trick, walking off with the apples, Prometheus freed on the same trip); Hesiod, Theogony 215-216 (the golden apples as Gaia's gift to Hera), 333-336 (Ladon the guardian); Pherecydes fragments (the earliest full narrative of the Atlas-and-shoulder-pad trick); Diodorus 4.26-27. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Hesperides' and 'Ladon (mythology)' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Apples of the Hesperides', 'Hesperides', 'Atlas (mythology)', 'Ladon (mythology)' -- Hesperides as evening-nymphs, tree a wedding gift from Gaia to Hera, hundred-headed serpent Ladon, Atlas holding up the sky, Heracles offering to hold it while Atlas picks the apples, Atlas trying to keep Heracles holding forever, Heracles's 'let me get a pad for my shoulders' trick, Prometheus freed on the same journey.
framing_note: The 'let me put a pad on my shoulders' ladder -- the trick is one of the great cleverness moments in Greek myth. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Atlas tried to leave Heracles holding the sky forever, and Heracles said 'sure, but hold this for just a MOMENT while I put a pad on my shoulders' -- and walked off) and T3 (the whole labor's trick is that only ATLAS can pick the apples, so Heracles has to take his job for a while). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem describe Heracles holding up the sky AND ask what happened -- describe the SCENE (a bent Titan at the world's edge, a garden guarded by a hundred-headed serpent, a request for help) and let the recall be the TRICK (asking Atlas to take the sky back 'just for a moment'), the GUARDIAN (the dragon Ladon), or the FRUIT (golden apples, Hera's wedding gift). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Odin drinking the mead by trickery, or of Loki tricking the dwarf into becoming a giant sneeze, or of Jack outfoxing the giant -- clever mortal beats vast eternal power. DISTRACTOR MINE: other golden apples (Aphrodite's apple that starts the Trojan War via the Judgment of Paris -- adjacent-real, must be distinguished; the golden apples Aphrodite gives Melanion to beat Atalanta -- adjacent-real from this same strand), other hundred-headed guards (Typhon; Argus Panoptes with a hundred eyes -- Hera's other guardian), other 'hold up the sky' Titans (Atlas is uniquely the sky-bearer). Wrong number of Hesperides: usually THREE (some sources four); the constellation from Ladon is DRACO.

Sister strand: Judgment of Paris (Aphrodite's apple) belongs to the Trojan War strand -- key DIFFERENT apples here (Hera's wedding-tree, not Eris's apple of discord).

name: Labor 12: Cerberus dragged up from Hades
scope: The last and impossible labor. T1: the TWELFTH and final LABOR, meant by Eurystheus to be lethal, is to bring back CERBERUS -- the THREE-HEADED (some sources fifty or a hundred, but the standard image is three) monstrous DOG who guards the gates of HADES, so no living soul can leave and no dead soul can escape. His father is Typhon, his mother Echidna; his brothers are Orthrus, the Hydra, and the Chimera. His neck writhes with serpents; his tail is a live snake. T2: no living human descends to Hades and returns. Heracles first has to be INITIATED at the Mysteries of ELEUSIS to be permitted; then HERMES (guide of souls) and ATHENA lead him down to the underworld through a cavern in the Peloponnese at Tainaron. T3: in Hades he meets many of the shades -- MELEAGER (whose sister Deianira Heracles will later marry, from Meleager's ghost's suggestion), MEDUSA's shade (from whom Athena stops him drawing his sword), and THESEUS and PIRITHOUS stuck to the Chair of Forgetfulness. He TEARS Theseus free by main force (some sources say pieces of Theseus's thighs remain stuck to the chair -- which is why Athenian men are said to have narrow thighs afterward); PIRITHOUS he cannot budge, and Pirithous stays in Hades forever. T4: Heracles goes before HADES and PERSEPHONE themselves and asks permission to take Cerberus; Hades agrees on one condition -- Heracles must SUBDUE the dog USING NO WEAPONS. Heracles wraps his lion-skin around him, grabs Cerberus around the neck, and squeezes until the great dog goes limp (Apollodorus 2.5.12). T5: he drags Cerberus up through a cavern at TROEZEN (or Heraclea, depending on source) and hauls the beast to Mycenae. Eurystheus, seeing three snapping heads coming at him, dives back into his BRONZE JAR one last time, and orders Heracles to take the dog straight back where he came from. Heracles brings Cerberus back to Hades. The twelve labors are complete. Where Cerberus's slaver dripped on Greek soil on the way up, the poisonous plant ACONITE (wolfsbane) is said to grow (Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.408-419). Further rungs: after the twelve labors are done Heracles goes on to further adventures -- the shirt of Nessus, Mount Oeta, his apotheosis to Olympus -- covered in their own ladder here; the Eleusinian Mysteries as a real cult are honored here as the prerequisite even for a hero of Zeus.

name: The shirt of Nessus: Heracles's last day on Mount Oeta
scope: The end of Heracles, brought about by his own long-ago arrow. T1: years after the twelve labors, Heracles marries a princess named DEIANIRA (sister of Meleager, the boar-hunter). Traveling home with her, they come to the flooded river EVENUS, and a centaur named NESSUS offers to carry Deianira across on his back while Heracles wades. In midstream Nessus tries to run off with her (Apollodorus 2.7.6-7; Sophocles, Trachiniae). T2: Heracles, on the far bank, draws his bow and shoots Nessus dead with one of his HYDRA-POISONED ARROWS -- the same arrows from the second labor. As Nessus lies dying, he speaks to Deianira and gives her a gift with a lie: he tells her to soak up some of his BLOOD (which is now full of Hydra-poison, but he does not say so), and if Heracles ever loves another woman, she can smear the blood on a garment and it will win his love back. Deianira, believing him, saves the poisoned blood in a jar and hides it. T3: years later Heracles brings home a captive princess named IOLE, and Deianira, fearing she is losing him, remembers Nessus's 'love-charm.' She soaks a beautiful new SHIRT (in Sophocles, a fine white ceremonial robe) in the centaur's blood and sends it to Heracles at his sacrifice on Cape Cenaeum in Euboea. T4: Heracles puts the shirt on. The Hydra-poison, activated by his own body-heat, BURNS INTO HIS SKIN -- when he tries to tear the shirt off, the flesh comes off with it (Sophocles, Trachiniae 1046-1075). His agony is so great he uproots trees. Deianira, realizing what she has done, kills herself. T5: knowing no cure exists, Heracles has his companions carry him to the top of Mount OETA, orders a great PYRE built of oak logs, lies down on it, and asks for the pyre to be lit. No one dares -- until his companion PHILOCTETES agrees to light it in exchange for Heracles's BOW AND POISONED ARROWS (the same arrows that will later, in Philoctetes's hands, kill Paris of Troy). The pyre burns; the MORTAL PART of Heracles burns away; the IMMORTAL PART, the Zeus-half, is carried up to Olympus, where Hera at last reconciles with him and gives him her daughter HEBE, cup-bearer of the gods, as bride (Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.229-272). Further rungs: the Hydra-poison thus completes a full circle -- from Labor 2 (Iolaus and the torch) to Heracles's own death; Sophocles's Trachiniae is the great Greek tragedy of this ending; the pyre on Mount Oeta was a real cult-site in later antiquity with reported burnt-earth layers; Philoctetes and the bow become the setup for Sophocles's other famous play and for the fall of Troy (the oracle said Troy could not fall without Heracles's bow).

Dinner-test payoff: T2/T3 (a dying centaur told Deianira his blood was a LOVE-CHARM; years later she smeared it on a shirt and sent it to her husband and it burned him to death) and T5 (his companion PHILOCTETES agreed to light the pyre in exchange for his BOW, and that bow would later kill Paris at Troy). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name the shirt AND ask what killed Heracles -- describe the SCENE (a river, a centaur, a wife promised a love-charm, a shirt at a sacrifice) and let the recall be the SOURCE of the poison (Nessus's blood, actually Hydra-poison from long ago), the wife (Deianira), or the mountain (Oeta). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Balder killed by his own brother with a mistletoe dart, or of Sigurd betrayed at the well, or of Cuchulainn dying tied to a stone -- the great hero brought down by a specific object rooted in his own earlier story. Kids can handle it (per stance rule -- Norse and Celtic myth are LOUD). DISTRACTOR MINE: other Heracles wives (Megara whom he killed in madness; Hebe on Olympus at the end -- adjacent, must be distinguished), other death-shirts in myth (the shirt of Medea for Glauce -- adjacent-real from the same Argonauts strand, must be distinguished), other centaurs (Chiron the tutor, Pholus, Nessus -- all three killed by the same Hydra-poison in different scenes across the cycle). Wrong flame-lighters: not Iolaus, not Hylas; PHILOCTETES.

name: Perseus and the gods' gift-list: kibisis, mirror, cap, sandals
scope: The equipment-quest at the start of the Gorgon adventure. T1: PERSEUS is the son of ZEUS and the mortal princess DANAE, whose father Acrisius (king of Argos) had shut her in a bronze tower after a prophecy said her son would kill him. Zeus came to her as a SHOWER OF GOLD through the roof; the baby Perseus was born. Acrisius shut mother and baby in a WOODEN CHEST and cast them out to sea; the chest washed up on the island of SERIFOS, and a kind fisherman named DICTYS took them in (Apollodorus 2.4.1-3). T2: years later, Dictys's brother King POLYDECTES wants Danae as his wife and Perseus in the way. He announces a pretended wedding and asks each guest for a wedding-present -- a HORSE. Perseus has no horse. Polydectes asks what he WILL give; Perseus, cornered, boasts he will bring the HEAD OF MEDUSA. Polydectes leaps on the promise and holds him to it. T3: Perseus, alone and unequipped against a monster whose gaze turns any who look at her to stone, is helped by two gods -- ATHENA and HERMES. Athena gives him a POLISHED BRONZE SHIELD (or in some sources a bronze MIRROR) so he can look at Medusa's reflection instead of her face. Hermes gives him a curved sickle-sword called the HARPE and lends him his own winged SANDALS to fly. T4: Athena tells him he must also get three special items from certain NYMPHS -- but no one knows where the nymphs live except the GRAEAE, three grey-haired sisters who share ONE EYE and ONE TOOTH between them, passing them back and forth. Perseus SNATCHES THE EYE as it is being passed and refuses to give it back until they tell him the way. T5: he goes to the nymphs and receives the THREE ITEMS: (1) the CAP OF INVISIBILITY of HADES ('kynee', darkness-cap -- the very same cap Hades wore in the Titanomachy); (2) a pair of WINGED SANDALS (in the versions where Hermes did not already lend his own); and (3) the KIBISIS, a special magical BAG able to safely contain the severed Gorgon-head, since the head keeps its stone-turning power after death. Now equipped, he flies west to the sleeping Gorgons. Further rungs: the three Gorgon sisters are Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa -- only Medusa is mortal; Perseus's whole kit is unusual for a hero because so much of it comes from FOUR different gods (Zeus his father, Athena, Hermes, Hades) plus the nymphs; the harpe sword is the same shape as the sickle Cronus used on Ouranos in Hesiod -- the Greek word 'harpe' is the same for both.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.1-2.4.5 (the chest on the sea, Serifos, Dictys, Polydectes's wedding-present trick, Perseus's boast, the harpe from Hermes, the shield from Athena, the Graeae and the eye, the nymphs and the cap of Hades / winged sandals / kibisis, the Gorgons); Hesiod, Shield of Heracles 216-237 (the harpe, the kibisis, the cap of Hades, the winged sandals -- all four items named); Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.610-803 (the whole Perseus cycle in Latin verse); Pindar, Pythian 10.29-48 and Pythian 12 (the head, the flying return). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the polished shield or a mirror is standard (both variants exist; Hesiod's Shield of Heracles has the polished shield).

Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the three grey witches shared ONE EYE and ONE TOOTH between them and Perseus SNATCHED the eye mid-pass to force them to talk) and T5 (his kit was four things -- HADES's cap of invisibility, WINGED sandals, a magic BAG called the kibisis, and Hermes's curved sword called the HARPE). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of the young Sigurd receiving Gram from Regin, or of Arthur's Excalibur from the Lady of the Lake, or of Robin Hood equipped with his longbow -- the specific magical equipment-catalog of a hero's launch. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Athena-gifts (the bronze rattle to Heracles -- adjacent-real from the same strand, must be distinguished), other winged-sandal wearers (Hermes himself; some sources give a pair to Perseus, some say Hermes just lends his own), other magical bags (the goatskin bag of Aeolus in the Odyssey -- adjacent, must be distinguished). Wrong swords: not Excalibur (Arthurian), not Gram (Sigurd's), not Durendal (Roland's) -- the HARPE, a curved sickle-sword.

name: Perseus at the Gorgon's cave: Medusa, Pegasus, Chrysaor
scope: The killing itself and the births from the neck. T1: the three GORGONS -- STHENO, EURYALE, and MEDUSA -- live at the edge of the world beyond the ocean-stream (some sources place them in Libya). Their heads are wreathed in living SNAKES instead of hair, their teeth are boar-tusks, their hands are bronze; anyone who looks at their FACES turns instantly to STONE. Two of the three -- Stheno and Euryale -- are IMMORTAL; only MEDUSA is mortal, and she is Perseus's target (Hesiod, Theogony 270-283). T2: Ovid tells the sad backstory: Medusa was once a beautiful mortal priestess of Athena; POSEIDON assaulted her in Athena's temple, and Athena, offended (in Ovid's telling, at Medusa, though this reads unkindly against a victim), turned her hair into snakes and her face into stone-turning horror (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.794-803). Older sources treat the Gorgons simply as ancient monsters without backstory. T3: Perseus flies in wearing the CAP OF HADES so the two immortal sisters cannot see him. He approaches Medusa AVERTING HIS EYES and using ATHENA's POLISHED SHIELD as a MIRROR to see her reflection safely. Guided by the reflection, he strikes with the HARPE and severs her head with one blow. T4: from the severed NECK spring two beings, sired earlier by Poseidon: (1) PEGASUS, the winged horse (later ridden by Bellerophon against the Chimera), and (2) CHRYSAOR, a warrior born already fully-armed carrying a golden sword (his name means 'golden sword'; he becomes the father of Geryon of the tenth labor). T5: Perseus stuffs the head into the KIBISIS while it still keeps its stone-power (it will turn people to stone for the rest of the story) and flies away. The two immortal sisters wake and pursue but cannot see him through the cap of invisibility. Later, in one common tradition, Athena takes the Gorgon-head from Perseus and sets it in the CENTRE OF HER AEGIS, where it remains for the rest of Greek myth as a battle-terror (Athena wears it on her breastplate, and Zeus's aegis carries the same face). Further rungs: the drops of blood from the severed head fall across the Libyan desert and turn into snakes, the origin-myth of North African serpents (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.617-620); the head's stone-power is used on Atlas (turned into the Atlas Mountains, per Ovid) and on Polydectes (see next rung); Athena's aegis with the Gorgon-face is the same aegis first seen in the Athena-birth ladder.
source: PRIMARY: Hesiod, Theogony 270-286 (the three Gorgons, Medusa alone mortal, Pegasus and Chrysaor born from her neck when Perseus struck); Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.610-803 (the mirror-shield use, the backstory of Medusa, the blood-drops making snakes, the head turning Atlas into a mountain); Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.2-3 (the killing, the head into the kibisis, the head later on Athena's aegis); Pindar, Pythian 12 (the beheading). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Medusa' and 'Pegasus' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Medusa', 'Gorgon', 'Pegasus', 'Chrysaor' -- three Gorgons at the world's edge, only Medusa mortal, snakes for hair, mirror-shield technique, cap of Hades for invisibility from the immortal sisters, Pegasus + Chrysaor born from the neck, head kept in the kibisis with lingering stone-power, later on Athena's aegis. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Chrysaor's specific 'golden sword' etymology is Hesiodic or later.

Dinner-test payoff: T4 (when Perseus struck off Medusa's head, out sprang the WINGED HORSE PEGASUS and a warrior called Chrysaor -- Poseidon's children by her, held inside until the neck opened) and T3 (he did not LOOK at her -- he watched her reflection in Athena's polished SHIELD). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Sigurd beheading Fafnir, or of David and Goliath -- monster-killing with a specific technique that becomes iconic. DISTRACTOR MINE: other snake-haired figures (the Furies with snakes in their hair -- adjacent-real, must be distinguished), other winged horses in myth (there is really only PEGASUS -- but wrong choices might name generic 'a Nemean horse'), other Poseidon-Medusa offspring (Chrysaor, whose son is Geryon of the tenth labor). Wrong number of Gorgons mortal: only ONE (Medusa) of THREE.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Libya as the traditional Gorgon-location and the North African desert whose snakes are said to come from Gorgon-blood; theology owns the beheading itself.

name: Andromeda on the rock and the stone king of Serifos
scope: The rescue on the way home and the return to Serifos. T1: flying home from the Gorgon's cave with Medusa's head in the kibisis, Perseus passes over the ETHIOPIAN COAST and sees a beautiful princess CHAINED NAKED TO A ROCK by the sea. She is ANDROMEDA, daughter of King CEPHEUS and Queen CASSIOPEIA -- and Cassiopeia had bragged that Andromeda was more beautiful than the sea-nymphs the NEREIDS. In offense, Poseidon sent a sea-monster called CETUS to eat the country's cattle and people. An oracle said only ANDROMEDA CHAINED AS A SACRIFICE would satisfy the monster (Apollodorus 2.4.3). T2: Perseus lands, learns the story, and asks Cepheus for Andromeda in marriage if he saves her; Cepheus agrees. T3: Cetus rises from the sea. Perseus flies down with his winged sandals and either (a) attacks with the HARPE from above and stabs it repeatedly (Ovid's version, Metamorphoses 4.717-740) or (b) turns it to stone by holding up the Gorgon head (later art, Roman version). In most tellings Ovid is followed and the sword-attack is the standard. T4: at the wedding feast, Andromeda's earlier fiance PHINEUS bursts in with an armed band claiming her back. Perseus, badly outnumbered, calls out for anyone on his side to look away -- and holds up MEDUSA'S HEAD from the kibisis. Phineus and all his men TURN TO STONE in mid-charge (Ovid describes them frozen in each posture -- one with a raised sword, one at the front lunge, one at the moment of flight). T5: Perseus and Andromeda return to SERIFOS. There he finds his mother DANAE has taken refuge in a temple to escape King Polydectes's advances; Perseus walks into Polydectes's hall where the king sits at feast, and holds up the head. Polydectes and his whole court are TURNED TO STONE where they sit (Apollodorus 2.4.3). Perseus makes kindly DICTYS (his childhood benefactor) king in Polydectes's place, and gives the harpe back to Hermes, the sandals and cap back to the nymphs, the polished shield and the Gorgon-head to ATHENA -- who sets the head in the centre of her aegis. Further rungs: Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Andromeda, Perseus and Cetus are all placed as CONSTELLATIONS in the night sky, all near each other -- Cassiopeia in her chair, upside-down half the year as her punishment; Perseus later accidentally kills his grandfather Acrisius with a badly-thrown discus at funeral games in Larissa, fulfilling the original prophecy; his sons found MYCENAE and Tiryns.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.3-2.4.5 (Andromeda chained, Cetus, the rescue, Phineus at the wedding turned to stone, return to Serifos, Polydectes turned to stone, kingdom to Dictys, gear returned to the gods, Athena putting the head on the aegis); Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.663-5.249 (the whole Andromeda cycle at length, especially 4.717-740 for the fight with Cetus and 5.1-235 for the Phineus stone-scene); Pindar, Pythian 12.11-27 (Perseus with the head); Herodotus 2.91 (Andromeda cult in Egypt). Wrong king turned to stone: not Cepheus (he is Andromeda's father, spared), not Phineus alone (he was already stoned earlier); POLYDECTES and his court at Serifos.

HISTORY owns the constellations of Perseus, Andromeda, Cassiopeia, Cepheus and Cetus as real IAU-recognized constellations still charted; theology owns why they are grouped together.

name: Theseus on the road to Athens: Sinis, Sciron, Procrustes
scope: The 'six labors' Theseus does on the way to meet his father, each killer killed by his own method. T1: THESEUS grows up at TROEZEN in his mother AETHRA's household not knowing who his father is. His mother's mysterious partner was actually KING AEGEUS of ATHENS (though in another tradition his father is POSEIDON, so Theseus is doubly-fathered). When Theseus is old enough, Aethra leads him to a great BOULDER and tells him to lift it. Under the boulder lie a SWORD and a pair of SANDALS Aegeus left as tokens; Theseus lifts the rock, takes the sword and sandals, and sets out for Athens (Plutarch, Life of Theseus 3-6). T2: he refuses to sail (the safe way) and insists on going by the DANGEROUS OVERLAND ROAD around the Saronic Gulf, which is infested with bandits. He kills each one BY THAT BANDIT'S OWN METHOD. First: PERIPHETES 'the Club-Bearer' at Epidaurus, who bludgeons travellers -- Theseus takes his brass club (and carries it for the rest of his life). T3: SINIS 'PINE-BENDER' bends two pine trees down to the ground, ties travellers between them, and lets the trees spring apart, tearing his victim in half. Theseus ties SINIS between his own two pines. Then the CROMMYONIAN SOW, a giant she-pig; then SCIRON on a narrow clifftop path, who forces travellers to WASH HIS FEET and then kicks them off the cliff into the sea below, where a GIANT SEA-TURTLE (some sources a tortoise) waits. Theseus kicks Sciron off his own cliff. T4: CERCYON at Eleusis, a wrestler who challenges every passer-by to a match and kills each opponent -- Theseus wrestles him to death (in the process inventing 'scientific' wrestling technique by using leverage rather than pure strength, according to Plutarch and Pausanias). T5: last and most famous is PROCRUSTES ('the Stretcher'), who runs an inn near Athens; he ties guests to an iron BED and MAKES THEM FIT -- stretching the short ones on a rack, LOPPING OFF the feet or head of the tall ones. Theseus ties PROCRUSTES on his own bed and 'makes him fit' by cutting off his head (Plutarch, Life of Theseus 11). Arriving in Athens as the killer of six road-monsters, he is welcomed as a hero -- and only then reveals to Aegeus the sword. Further rungs: the phrase 'a Procrustean bed' has entered every modern European language as a synonym for a rigid framework forced on things that don't fit; Theseus's early career of killing each bandit by his own method is a poetic-justice pattern Greek storytellers loved; the boulder at Troezen was still shown to travellers in Pausanias's day (Pausanias 2.32.7); the sea-turtle at Sciron's cliff is one of the few sea-turtle appearances in Greek myth.
source: PRIMARY: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 3-11 (the boulder at Troezen, sword and sandals, insistence on the overland route, all six bandits in order -- Periphetes, Sinis, the Crommyonian Sow, Sciron and the turtle, Cercyon, Procrustes and the bed -- each killed by his own method); Apollodorus, Epitome 1.1-4 (parallel prose); Pausanias 2.32.7 (the boulder still shown), 1.44.8 (Sciron's cliff). name: Theseus, Ariadne's thread, and the black sails Aegeus saw
scope: The Labyrinth story and the naming of the Aegean Sea. T1: Athens is under a terrible tribute to King MINOS of Crete: every nine years (some sources every year), SEVEN YOUNG MEN AND SEVEN YOUNG WOMEN must sail to Crete to be fed to the MINOTAUR -- the bull-headed monster (child of Pasiphae and the Cretan Bull from the seventh Labor of Heracles) that Minos keeps in the LABYRINTH designed by DAEDALUS. THESEUS volunteers himself as one of the seven young men and sails with the tribute, promising his father AEGEUS that on his return the ship will change her BLACK MOURNING SAILS for WHITE SAILS if he is alive (Plutarch, Life of Theseus 15-17). T2: at Knossos, King Minos's daughter ARIADNE sees Theseus and falls in love; she goes to Daedalus for advice, and Daedalus gives her a BALL OF THREAD (the 'clew' -- the word 'clue' in English comes from this, a 'clew of thread' being originally the way to find your way home). Ariadne meets Theseus at night, gives him a sword and the clew, and tells him: TIE ONE END TO THE DOOR-POST OF THE LABYRINTH and let the ball unwind as you go in. T3: Theseus enters the Labyrinth, letting the thread play out behind him, penetrating deeper and deeper into the maze. In the innermost chamber he finds the MINOTAUR and kills it -- in most sources with the sword Ariadne gave him, in some sources with his BARE HANDS after his sword breaks. He then follows the thread back to the entrance and leads the fourteen Athenians out to freedom. T4: he sails away with Ariadne and the Athenian youths. On the island of NAXOS he abandons Ariadne asleep on the beach (in some versions Dionysus appears and takes her as his own bride, so the abandonment is divine-mandated; in others Theseus is simply cruel). Sailing on, in his GRIEF and DISTRACTION he FORGETS to change the black sails for white. T5: at Athens, AEGEUS is waiting on the CLIFFS at Cape SOUNION scanning the horizon every day. When he sees the ship approaching under BLACK SAILS, he believes his son is dead, and in despair THROWS HIMSELF FROM THE CLIFF INTO THE SEA -- and that sea is called the AEGEAN SEA to this day, in his memory (Plutarch, Life of Theseus 22; Pausanias 1.22.5). Theseus lands, learns what has happened, and becomes king of Athens. Further rungs: the WORD 'clue' in English literally comes from Ariadne's 'clew' of thread -- the way through a mystery back to the start; Daedalus who designed the Labyrinth later escapes Crete with his son Icarus on wax wings (Icarus flies too close to the sun and falls -- a separate famous story); Ariadne on Naxos is one of the great subjects of ancient and later art, from Titian to Strauss.
source: PRIMARY: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 15-23 (the tribute, the volunteering, Ariadne's love, Daedalus's advice, the thread, the Minotaur, the sails, Aegeus leaping); Apollodorus, Epitome 1.7-11 (the whole cycle in prose); Diodorus 4.61; Pausanias 1.22.5 (Aegeus's leap from Sounion, the sea named); Ovid, Heroides 10 (Ariadne's own letter from Naxos to Theseus). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the tribute was every nine years (Plutarch) or every year (Apollodorus).
framing_note: The 'why the sea is called the Aegean' ladder -- the sail-color mistake is the payoff every child should know. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (Theseus FORGOT to change the black sails for white, his father saw the black sails from the cliff and jumped, and the sea is called the AEGEAN because of it) and T2 (Ariadne gave him a ball of THREAD tied to the door-post -- and the English word 'CLUE' comes from that ball). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name the Aegean AND ask which sea -- describe the SCENE (a father on a cliff, a ship approaching under the wrong-colored sails, a leap) and let the recall be the SEA (Aegean), the KING (Aegeus), or the thread-giver (Ariadne). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Roland refusing to blow the Olifant until too late at Roncesvalles, or of Peter's cock-crow -- a single missed signal that ends a life. DISTRACTOR MINE: other named seas of Greek myth (Ionian sea named after Io, Icarian sea after Icarus -- adjacent-real, must be distinguished), other 'father waiting' scenes, other Minotaur-related figures (Daedalus, Icarus, Ariadne, Phaedra -- Ariadne's sister whom Theseus marries later). Wrong helpers with the thread: not Daedalus directly (though he told her how), not Minos (his father); ARIADNE. Wrong bull-monster: Minotaur (right), not the Cretan Bull itself (which is Heracles's Labor 7, its father).

HISTORY owns Athens's actual Bronze-Age tributary relations with Minoan Crete; theology owns the Minotaur legend. LANGUAGE: 'clue' etymology.

name: Theseus and Pirithous stuck to the Chair of Forgetfulness
scope: The over-reach that ends Theseus's active career. T1: after his kingship at Athens, Theseus makes a great sworn friendship with PIRITHOUS, king of the LAPITHS of Thessaly. The two make a pact: each will help the other find a WIFE. Theseus first -- Pirithous helps him carry off the young HELEN OF SPARTA (yes, the future Helen of Troy), then still a child; Theseus takes her home and leaves her with his mother Aethra. Now it is Pirithous's turn. T2: Pirithous, having lost his wife HIPPODAMIA (killed at the great CENTAUR WEDDING BRAWL when a centaur tried to abduct her -- another famous scene), announces that HE will marry PERSEPHONE, queen of the underworld and wife of HADES. Theseus, bound by his oath, agrees to help him. T3: the two friends descend to Hades through a cave (in some sources at Cape Tainaron, in others at Colonus outside Athens). They are welcomed politely by Hades himself, who offers them SEATS at his table (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24). T4: as soon as they sit down, they discover the seats are the CHAIRS OF FORGETFULNESS (thronoi lethes) -- and their bodies GROW INTO the stone, their memories fade, they cannot rise. Hades has trapped them without a fight; they sit in the underworld unable to move (Diodorus 4.63). T5: years later HERACLES, on his TWELFTH LABOR to fetch Cerberus, finds them sitting there. He grabs THESEUS by the arm and TEARS him bodily off the chair (in some traditions leaving pieces of his THIGHS stuck to the stone -- which is why Athenian men afterwards were said to have narrow thighs, a folk-etymology). Heracles reaches for PIRITHOUS, but the earth SHAKES and Persephone forbids it: Pirithous, who conceived the outrage, MUST STAY. Pirithous remains stuck to the chair in Hades forever. Theseus returns to the upper world but his kingship is broken -- he has been away too long, Athens has turned against him, and he eventually dies exiled on the island of SCYROS, pushed off a cliff by King LYCOMEDES (Plutarch, Life of Theseus 35). Further rungs: the Athenian general Cimon later recovered what were said to be Theseus's bones from Scyros and brought them home in 475 BCE -- one of the few hero-cults with a historical relic-return; Helen was eventually recovered by her Spartan brothers Castor and Pollux, who invaded Attica to get her back (Herodotus 9.73); the theme of 'seat that will not let you rise' echoes in Christian and Norse traditions (chairs of judgment, Odin's Hlidskjalf).
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.23-24 (the Pirithous friendship, the Helen abduction, the plan to carry off Persephone, descent to Hades, the trap of the seats, Heracles later freeing Theseus but not Pirithous); Diodorus 4.63 (the Chair of Forgetfulness, Persephone forbidding Pirithous's release); Plutarch, Life of Theseus 31-35 (Helen and the abduction plan, the descent, the recovery of Theseus by Heracles, the exile on Scyros, the death from Lycomedes); Homer, Odyssey 11.631 (Odysseus in the underworld sees the shades but avoids Theseus and Pirithous). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Hades gave them SEATS -- and the seats were the Chair of Forgetfulness, and their flesh GREW INTO the stone) and T5 (Heracles later found them there and TORE Theseus free, leaving strips of thigh-flesh stuck to the chair, but Persephone forbade freeing Pirithous, who is still there). Wrong friend of Theseus for the descent: not Heracles (he later RESCUES Theseus); PIRITHOUS is the one who conceived the plan.

name: Jason, the one sandal, and the Argo built by Argus
scope: The prophecy, the ship, and the outbound voyage to Colchis. T1: JASON is the rightful heir to the throne of IOLCUS in Thessaly. His uncle PELIAS has usurped the kingdom, and Jason's parents smuggled the baby out to be raised in secret by the wise centaur CHIRON on Mount Pelion. Chiron also raises Asclepius, Achilles, and other future heroes -- a Who's-Who nursery. T2: Pelias had received a prophecy: 'BEWARE A MAN WEARING ONLY ONE SANDAL.' Years later Jason returns as a young man to claim his throne; on the road he meets an old woman at a swollen river and carries her across on his back -- LOSING ONE OF HIS SANDALS in the current. The old woman is HERA in disguise (Pelias is her enemy) and this earns Jason her lifelong help. He arrives in Iolcus wearing ONE sandal. Pelias, remembering the oracle, cannot risk open murder; instead he sends Jason on an impossible errand -- fetch the GOLDEN FLEECE from KING AEETES of COLCHIS at the eastern end of the Black Sea (Apollodorus 1.9.16). T3: the ship is built by the shipwright ARGUS with help from Athena; it is named the ARGO after its builder, and its crew are called the ARGONAUTS. Its prow-timber is a piece of the SPEAKING OAK of DODONA (the tree of Zeus's oracle), given by Athena -- so the ship herself can PROPHESY. The crew is the greatest gathering of heroes in one place before Troy: Heracles for a while, ORPHEUS with his lyre, the twins CASTOR and POLLUX, ATALANTA (in some accounts), MELEAGER, LAERTES (father of Odysseus), TELAMON and PELEUS (fathers of Ajax and Achilles), the winged sons of the North Wind CALAIS and ZETES. T4: at the Bosporus they come to the CLASHING ROCKS -- the SYMPLEGADES -- two mountainous cliffs that CRASH together every few seconds, crushing anything between them, then open to reset. The blind prophet PHINEUS (whom Calais and Zetes had earlier saved from the HARPIES who were snatching his food) tells them the trick: RELEASE A DOVE first; if the dove makes it through, row through hard on her tail. The dove flies -- the rocks crash -- lose only her tail-feathers. The Argo rows through as they part again -- the stern-post is nicked but she is through. After that passage the Symplegades are FIXED in place forever, never to move again (Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 2.549-609). T5: through the Black Sea to Colchis. King Aeetes agrees to give up the Fleece if Jason will YOKE two FIRE-BREATHING BRONZE-HOOFED BULLS to a plow, then plow a field, then sow it with DRAGON'S TEETH from which armed warriors will spring up, then fight them. It is meant to kill him. His secret advantage is that Aeetes's daughter MEDEA has fallen in love with him and is a great sorceress (see the next Medea rung). Further rungs: the shipwright ARGUS also carved a figurehead of Athena into the prow around the speaking-oak plank; the Symplegades ceasing to clash is one of Greek myth's clever 'permanent change of the world' beats, like Perseus's blood-drops making Libyan snakes; Phineus's Harpies were driven off by Calais and Zetes the Boreads (winged), a rare labor for a subsidiary Argonaut.

Wrong ship-carpenter: not Daedalus (Labyrinth); ARGUS the shipwright.

name: Medea in Colchis and the cauldron at Iolcus
scope: The three impossible tasks, the sleepless dragon, the murder in the strait, and Medea's revenge on Pelias. T1: MEDEA, sorceress-priestess of HECATE, daughter of KING AEETES of Colchis and the sea-nymph Idyia, sees Jason arrive and falls hopelessly in love (Hera and Aphrodite arrange this). She meets him secretly at the temple of Hecate and gives him a magical OINTMENT to smear on his skin and weapons, protecting him from fire and iron for one day (Apollonius, Argonautica 3.828-878). T2: the first task -- YOKE THE FIRE-BREATHING BULLS. Aeetes's bulls have BRONZE HOOVES and breathe fire; they have never been yoked. Protected by Medea's ointment, Jason walks into their pen, wrestles each bull down, and yokes them to Aeetes's iron plow. T3: the second task -- SOW THE DRAGON'S TEETH. From every tooth that Jason plants in the ploughed field springs a fully-armed WARRIOR ('the Spartoi', 'sown men'). Medea has told him what to do: he PICKS UP A ROCK and throws it into the middle of them. Not knowing who threw it, they turn on each other and cut each other down until none is left standing (Apollonius, Argonautica 3.1354-1407). T4: Aeetes refuses to give up the Fleece anyway. That night Medea leads Jason to the sacred GROVE OF ARES where the Fleece hangs on a tree, guarded by an enormous SERPENT/DRAGON that NEVER SLEEPS. Medea sings a lullaby-charm and sprinkles the beast's eyes with juice of magic herbs; the sleepless dragon SLEEPS for the first time in its life. Jason takes the Fleece from the tree. T5: they flee at dawn with Aeetes's fleet in pursuit. To slow the pursuit, MEDEA MURDERS HER OWN LITTLE BROTHER APSYRTUS (whom she had brought aboard), chops him into pieces, and scatters the pieces on the sea -- Aeetes stops his warships to gather up the body-parts of his son for burial, and the Argo escapes (Apollodorus 1.9.24). At Iolcus, to punish PELIAS for the original usurpation and for the death of Jason's parents, Medea shows Pelias's daughters a trick: she chops up an old RAM, boils him in a CAULDRON with magic herbs, and out springs a young lamb. Convinced, the daughters (led by ALCESTIS) chop up their old father Pelias and boil him in the same cauldron -- but Medea does not add the herbs. Pelias STAYS DEAD. Further rungs: Medea and Jason are exiled from Iolcus for the murder; they go to Corinth where Jason later abandons Medea for Glauce (King Creon's daughter) and Medea takes her REVENGE -- she sends Glauce a poisoned WEDDING DRESS that burns her alive (the shirt-of-Nessus pattern), and kills her own children by Jason (this is Euripides's Medea 431 BCE); Jason's own end is quiet -- he wanders back to Iolcus and dies when a ROTTING BEAM of the beached ARGO falls on him as he sleeps in her shadow; the Fleece hangs on afterward at Colchis in most sources, later becoming the emblem of the Order of the Golden Fleece founded by Philip the Good of Burgundy in 1430.
source: PRIMARY: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica Book 3 (Medea falling in love, the ointment, the fire-bulls, the dragon's teeth, the sown warriors) and Book 4 (the sleepless dragon lulled, the flight, the murder of Apsyrtus); Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.9.23-1.9.28 (parallel prose, especially the cauldron trick on Pelias and the daughters); Euripides, Medea 431 BCE (Glauce's poisoned dress, the killing of the children); Pindar, Pythian 4.213-250 (Medea's aid); Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.159-293 (the rejuvenation trick with the ram and cauldron); Homer, Odyssey 12.70 (the Argo as 'known to all men'). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name Medea AND ask who helped Jason -- describe the SCENE (a princess-sorceress meeting a stranger at a temple of Hecate, a coating for the skin, a dragon that never sleeps) and let the recall be the HELPER (Medea), the FEAT (lulling the sleepless dragon, throwing a rock among the sown warriors), or the horror (chopping the brother, boiling Pelias). Kids can handle it (per stance rule -- both Norse and Celtic myth are LOUD, as is Greek).
